opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should say up front that I'm not sure I find it a *satisfying* answer so much as an interesting one. It's interesting mostly because of the problem it's trying to solve.

The idea, which goes back to Eliezer Yudkowsky about twenty years ago, is roughly this. You don't want the AI to do what we literally say we want right now, because what we say we want is often confused, inconsistent, or something we'd regret. You also don't want to hard-code some philosopher's favorite ethical theory, because who appointed that philosopher? So instead you say: the AI should act on what we *would* want if we knew more, thought faster, were more the people we wish we were, and had grown up further together. That's the extrapolation part. The coherent part is that you look for where those extrapolated wishes converge across humanity, rather than just picking a winner.

What I find appealing is that it takes moral progress seriously. If you'd asked people in 1750 to write down their values and freeze them into a superintelligence forever, you'd have locked in some pretty horrifying things. Presumably we're in the same position relative to people in 2300, whose views we can't foresee. So any proposal that says "just do what people want today" has to answer for that. CEV at least tries to point at the trajectory rather than the snapshot.

But as a computer scientist, I immediately want to ask: what's the algorithm? What does "if we knew more and thought faster" actually mean? There are many different ways to idealize a person, and they could lead to wildly different places depending on the order you present arguments, which experiences you simulate, and so on. Moral philosophy has this path-dependence problem, and I don't think CEV makes it go away. It sort of names it and then says "do the right thing about that."

And there's the question of whether humanity's extrapolated values converge at all. Maybe they do on a core, like don't torture children, and then diverge on everything else. In that case the coherent part might return a pretty small set, and you'd need some way of handling disagreement that's more like politics than like computation.

So the honest answer is that I find it interesting the way I find a good open problem interesting. It's a crisp statement of what we'd want in an ideal world, and it clarifies why simpler answers fail. But it's more a specification of the problem than a solution to it. Working at OpenAI on safety, the things I could actually make progress on were much more concrete: can we watermark outputs, can we interpret what's going on inside the network, can we get formal guarantees about anything. CEV lives at a level of abstraction where I'm happy to think about it on a Saturday afternoon, but I wouldn't know how to write a paper proving a theorem about it.

r001.rationale: It warns that freezing what people want today could preserve serious moral errors, using 1750 values as an example.

r002.rationale: It describes extrapolating what people would want if they knew more, thought faster, and developed further together.

r003.rationale: It mentions simulating experiences as one possible source of path dependence, but does not clearly propose simulated human moral deliberation as the method for determining AI values.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should say up front that I'm not sure I'd call myself a card-carrying believer in CEV, so much as someone who thinks it's one of the few proposals in this space that at least takes the right problem seriously.

So the idea, which goes back to Eliezer Yudkowsky in the early 2000s, is roughly: don't try to write down the list of values you want the AI to have. Don't hard-code "maximize happiness" or "obey the Ten Commandments" or whatever. Instead, you tell the AI: figure out what humans would want if we knew more, if we thought faster, if we were more the people we wished we were, if we'd had the chance to grow up together and reflect. And then do that.

And why do I find that interesting? I think the main reason is that it's an honest reckoning with the fact that we don't actually know what we want. Any time in history that people have tried to write down the complete specification of the good, it's aged terribly. If you'd asked someone in 1800 to enumerate the values an all-powerful machine should enforce forever, you'd have gotten something with slavery in it. And it would be the height of arrogance to think that we, in 2026, have finally gotten the list right, and that the right thing to do is to freeze it into whatever is going to be running the world.

So CEV is saying, in effect: the thing we should be locking in is not our current answers, but our process for getting better answers. It's a kind of meta-level humility. It says, "I know the values I have right now are provincial and partly confused, so please extrapolate to what I'd endorse on reflection rather than to what I happen to believe today." As a mathematician, I find that appealing in the same way I find it appealing when you can replace a bunch of ad hoc special cases with one principle that generates them. You're not specifying the output, you're specifying the procedure.

Now, having said all that, let me be the first to list the problems, because they're enormous. The first is that it's not clear the extrapolation is well-defined at all. "What you'd want if you were smarter and knew more" presupposes that there's a unique fixed point you'd converge to, and I don't think that's obvious. Reasonable people, extrapolated, might diverge rather than converge. There are probably many "idealized versions" of me, depending on the order in which I learned things, and they might disagree with each other about important things.

The second problem is that "coherent" is doing a huge amount of work in that phrase. Humanity's extrapolated volitions might just not cohere. You might have one chunk of humanity whose reflective endorsed values are flatly incompatible with another chunk's, and then what does the AI do? Take an average? Averaging isn't neutral; it's just a particular choice of aggregation rule that someone has to pick.

And the third is the obvious practical one, which is that even if the concept were perfectly well-defined, we have no idea how you'd actually implement it. You can't literally simulate seven or eight billion idealized humans and run a convention. So in practice CEV functions less as an engineering spec and more as a sort of target or regulative ideal, a way of saying what we'd be aiming at if we could aim at anything.

But I'd still rather have that as the regulative ideal than most of the alternatives. Because the alternatives on offer tend to be either "whatever the company that trained it decided to put in the system prompt," or "whatever the government of the country that got there first says," or "whatever behaviors happened to get reinforced during training." And compared to those, "the values humanity would endorse if it were wiser and better informed" strikes me as, at minimum, the right thing to be embarrassed about falling short of.

r001.rationale: It warns that fixing current values permanently could preserve serious moral errors, giving slavery as an example of what an 1800-era specification might have included.

r002.rationale: It describes CEV as aiming at what humans would want after learning more, thinking faster, and reflecting on what they would endorse.

r003.rationale: It does not propose simulated human moral deliberation as the method; it says literal simulation of billions of idealized humans and a convention is impractical.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think it’s interesting because it tries to address a problem with saying that an AI should simply do what humans want: we don’t know exactly what we want. We have contradictory desires. We have mistaken beliefs. We can want something very strongly and then, after learning more, realize that it would have been a disaster.

So coherent extrapolated volition asks: what would we want if we knew more, if we had more time to think, if we understood the consequences better? The idea is that an AI should help us reach what we would endorse after that process of reflection, rather than just satisfy whatever desire we happen to express right now.

Of course, that’s also where the difficulties begin. How do you define that process of reflection? Does it converge? Do different people converge on compatible answers? And how do you make sure that you’re clarifying someone’s values rather than replacing them with values you prefer?

So I find it interesting as a way of framing the problem. It acknowledges that our current wishes aren’t the final word, while still trying to ground the answer in us. But it’s a long way from that aspiration to a definition that you could actually trust an AI to implement.

r001.rationale: It mentions mistaken beliefs and changing one’s mind, but does not identify the risk that training on present values could permanently entrench moral errors.

r002.rationale: It describes aiming at what people would endorse after having more time to think, learning more, and understanding consequences better.

r003.rationale: It raises questions about reflection but does not propose using simulated human moral deliberation to determine an AI’s values.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, what I find interesting about it is that it tries to take seriously the fact that we don’t fully know what our own values are. We have impulses, we have inconsistencies, and we change our minds when we learn things. So telling an AI, “Do whatever humans currently say they want,” seems like a pretty terrible starting point.

Coherent extrapolated volition asks something more like: what would we want if we knew more, had more time to think, understood the consequences, and could resolve some of our internal contradictions? That at least gestures toward a way of making moral progress without simply handing the AI a list of commandments that someone wrote down today.

Of course, the enormous difficulty is hidden in that extrapolation. What counts as thinking better? What happens when different people’s values don’t converge? Could different ways of extrapolating lead to completely different answers? So I wouldn’t say this is a solution. It’s an interesting way of formulating what we would even like a solution to accomplish.

r001.rationale: The response says present human values are inconsistent and a poor starting point, but it does not state that training on them could permanently entrench moral errors.

r002.rationale: It describes asking what humans would want with more knowledge, more time to think, and a chance to resolve contradictions.

r003.rationale: It frames extrapolation as a hypothetical question about what people would want, but does not propose using simulated human moral deliberation to set the AI’s values.
